questions.question: In an extensive-form game $\Gamma$, which objects form a subgame?
options: A single decision node $x$ with all its successors, whatever the information sets of $x$ and of all the nodes below it are.
An information set of some player together with all successors of the nodes of that information set.
Any connected part of the tree that contains at least one decision node and all of its terminal successors.
A single decision node $x$ with all its successors, such that no information set has nodes both inside and outside it.

questions.question: Is an extensive-form game $\Gamma$, starting at its root, a subgame of itself?
options: No: a subgame must start at a node other than the root, after at least one move has been made.
Only if $\Gamma$ has perfect information, since otherwise some information set of $\Gamma$ contains several nodes.
Only if no move of Nature occurs, since a chance move at the root cannot start a subgame.
Yes: the root is a singleton, and $\Gamma$ contains all its successors and every information set whole.

questions.question: Player 2's information set $h$ contains two decision nodes, $y_1$ and $y_2$. Can a subgame start at $y_1$?
options: Yes: every decision node starts a subgame, whatever information set it belongs to.
Yes, provided the subgame also contains $y_2$ and its successors as well as the successors of $y_1$.
No: player 2 at $y_1$ does not know she is at $y_1$, so the part below it is not a game of its own.
No, but only because $y_1$ and $y_2$ may be followed by different payoffs for player 2.

questions.question: Player 1 moves at a singleton node $x$ with actions $L$ and $R$, each followed by further moves. A student takes $x$, the branch after $L$ and all its successors, but leaves out the branch after $R$. Is this a subgame?
options: No: a subgame contains all successors of its starting node, including the branch after $R$.
Yes: it starts at the singleton $x$ and contains every node after $L$, cutting no information set.
Yes, provided no player who moves after $R$ also moves somewhere in the branch after $L$.
No: a subgame ends after one round of moves, so the further moves after $L$ must be dropped.

questions.question: In the entry game, the entrant chooses Out (game ends) or In; after In, the incumbent, who has observed entry, chooses Accommodate or Fight. How many subgames does the game have?

A two-player simultaneous-move game is drawn as a tree: player 1 chooses $T$ or $B$, and player 2 then chooses $L$ or $R$ without observing player 1, so player 2's two nodes form one information set. How many subgames does the tree have?
Nature first chooses Good or Bad weather. Player 1 observes the weather and then chooses $x$ or $y$, after which the game ends. How many subgames does this game have?

In the entry game, the entrant chooses Out or In, and after In the incumbent chooses Accommodate or Fight. Consider the strategy profile (Out, Fight). Which profile does it induce on the subgame that starts at the incumbent's node?
options: The incumbent plays Accommodate.
The incumbent plays Fight.
None, since the node is not reached.
The entrant plays Out, then Fight.

questions.question: Why does the definition of a subgame require that, whenever a node belongs to it, every node of that node's information set belongs to it too?
options: Otherwise a mover there would not know if play is inside the subgame, so it could not stand alone.
Otherwise the subgame might not contain any terminal node, and payoffs would not be defined in it.
Otherwise the subgame would contain nodes of more than one player, which a subgame may not do.
Otherwise a subgame could be reached on some plays but not on others, depending on strategies.

questions.question: In the entry game, the entrant chooses Out (game ends) or In; after In the incumbent chooses Accommodate or Fight. Under the profile (Out, Fight), the incumbent's node is never reached. Is the part of the tree after In still a subgame?
options: No: a subgame must be reached with positive probability when the given strategy profile is played.
Yes: subgames are defined by the tree, so being off the path does not matter.
Yes, but only because the incumbent's threat to Fight is credible.
No: unreached parts of the tree are dropped before subgames are counted.

questions.question: Let $\Gamma'$ be a subgame of an extensive-form game $\Gamma$, and let $\Gamma''$ be a subgame of $\Gamma'$ (with the information sets $\Gamma'$ inherits). Is $\Gamma''$ a subgame of $\Gamma$?
options: No: $\Gamma''$ is a subgame of $\Gamma'$ only, and must be checked again from scratch against all of $\Gamma$.
Yes: $\Gamma'$ keeps whole information sets of $\Gamma$, so $\Gamma''$ starts at a singleton of $\Gamma$ and cuts nothing.
Only if $\Gamma'$ is the whole game $\Gamma$, since otherwise the information sets of $\Gamma$ inside it may be split.
Only if $\Gamma''$ starts at a node of the same player who moves at the first node of $\Gamma'$.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $L$ or $R$. After $L$, player 2 observes this and chooses $a$ or $b$, and the game ends. After $R$, player 2 observes this and chooses $c$ or $d$; then player 3 moves without observing player 2's choice, so her two nodes form one information set. How many subgames are there?

In a finite game of perfect information, player 1 chooses $L$ or $R$; after $L$ player 2 chooses $a$ or $b$; after $R$ player 2 chooses $c$ or $d$; after $(R,c)$ player 1 chooses $x$ or $y$. All other choices end the game. How many subgames are there?
A student claims: "If an extensive-form game has imperfect information, its only subgame is the whole game." Which statement about this claim is correct?
options: False: an outside option followed by a simultaneous stage has imperfect information and $2$ subgames.
True: any non-singleton information set prevents every node except the root from starting a subgame.
True: subgames other than the whole game exist only in games where every information set is a singleton.
False: in imperfect-information games every decision node still starts a subgame of its own.

questions.question: A decision node $x$ of an extensive-form game forms a singleton information set. Which statement about whether $x$ starts a subgame is correct?
options: Being a singleton is sufficient: every singleton node starts a subgame, whatever lies below it in the tree.
Being a singleton is neither necessary nor sufficient: subgames may also start at nodes that lie in larger information sets.
Being a singleton is necessary but not sufficient: no node below $x$ may share an information set with a node outside.
Being a singleton is sufficient once the mover at $x$ moves again later, observing all moves in between.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $L$ or $R$. After $L$, player 2 (at a singleton node $y$) chooses $u$ or $d$. Then player 3 moves without observing anything: her nodes after $(L,u)$, after $(L,d)$ and after $R$ form one information set. How many subgames are there?

Player 1 chooses $L$ or $R$; player 2, without observing this, chooses $l$ or $r$. Player 1 then observes player 2's choice, remembers her own, and chooses $x$ or $y$; the game then ends. How many subgames are there?
Player 1 chooses $O$ or $F$; player 2 observes this choice and then chooses $o$ or $f$, after which the game ends (a sequential Battle of the Sexes). How many proper subgames does this game have?
